lpie-ayuda.title: Shell builtin or external program, and locating a lost file
lpie-ayuda.briefing:
You are asked to resolve three day-to-day queries (you need `sudo` for the last one):
1. Use the shell itself to find out what `cd` is and save the complete answer in `tipo-cd.txt`.
2. Do the same with `mkdir` and save it in `tipo-mkdir.txt`; the output must show where the program lives.
3. Somewhere on the system there is a file called `tesoro-perdido.txt`. Update the `locate` database and save only its absolute path in `ruta.txt`.
Your terminal opens in the challenge directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r010-ayuda`); files requested without a path go there.
lpie-ayuda.blind_alert: REQUEST [LOCATION] · You need to find out what type of commands the two commands are and find a missing file on the server.
hints: The shell can distinguish commands that are built into it from programs that live on disk: ask it, not a file finder.
`type NOMBRE` answers the first and second queries. For the third, `locate` searches a database that is only refreshed by a command in the `locate` family, and that command requires privileges.
`type cd > tipo-cd.txt`; `type mkdir > tipo-mkdir.txt`; `sudo updatedb`; `locate tesoro-perdido > ruta.txt`.
lpie-ayuda.solution_summary: `type` indicates whether a command is a shell builtin (`cd` is a builtin) or an external program with its path (`/usr/bin/mkdir`). `locate` queries a database that `updatedb` (as root) refreshes, so you have to update it before searching for a newly created file.

checks.ruta.txt tiene la ruta absoluta del teso: ruta.txt has the absolute path to the treasure

lpie-listar.title: Inspecting a personal folder: hidden files, sizes, and tree
lpie-listar.briefing:
You are asked to inventory the `casa/` folder, which contains visible files, hidden files, and subfolders:
1. Save into `ocultos.txt` the names of the hidden files in `casa/` (those starting with a dot), one per line and without `.` or `..`.
2. Save into `grande.txt` only the name of the largest file in `casa/`.
3. Save into `arbol.txt` the recursive listing of `casa/`, including all its subfolders.
4. Enter `casa/documentos/2024` and save its absolute path into `donde.txt`.
Your terminal opens in the challenge directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r010-listar`); files requested without a path go there.
lpie-listar.blind_alert: REQUEST [INVENTORY] · You need to produce a quick inventory of the contents of a sample personal folder.
hints: Each part is a variant of the command that lists directories: one option for hidden files, another to sort by size, another to recurse through subfolders. The absolute path is given by another command when you are inside.

Hidden files appear with the option that shows almost everything (without `.` or `..`) and you may need to filter the result. Sorting by size puts the largest first; to keep one line, use `head`. For `donde.txt`, enter the folder and run `pwd`.
`ls -A casa | grep '^\.' > ocultos.txt`; `ls -S casa | head -1 > grande.txt`; `ls -R casa > arbol.txt`; `cd casa/documentos/2024 && pwd > /home/alumno/retos/r010-listar/donde.txt`.
lpie-listar.solution_summary: `ls -A` lists everything except `.` and `..` (a `grep '^\.'` keeps only hidden entries), `ls -S` sorts from largest to smallest, `ls -R` recurses, and `pwd` prints the absolute path of the current directory after a `cd`.

lpie-ficheros.title: Reorganizing a project: create, copy, rename, move, and delete
lpie-ficheros.briefing:
You are asked to reorganize the working directory:
1. Create the path `proyecto/src/viejo` in a single command, with all intermediate folders.
2. Copy the entire `plantilla/` folder, with all its contents, as `proyecto/doc`.
3. Rename `borrador.txt` to `final.txt`.
4. Move only `dia1.log` … `dia9.log` (single digit) to `proyecto/src`, using a wildcard; `dia10.log` and `dia11.log` must stay where they are.
5. Delete the `basura/` folder with everything it contains.
Your terminal opens in the challenge directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r010-ficheros`); files requested without a path go there.
lpie-ficheros.blind_alert: REQUEST [ORGANIZATION] · You need to reorganize a project structure and clean up what is left over.
hints: Five file management operations: create a folder tree, copy folders, rename, move by pattern, and delete recursively. Watch out for the wildcard in item four.

Creating intermediate paths and copying folders each have a specific option in their command. A wildcard that represents exactly one character tells `dia9.log` apart from `dia10.log`. Renaming is moving to the same directory with a different name.
`mkdir -p proyecto/src/viejo`; `cp -r plantilla proyecto/doc`; `mv borrador.txt final.txt`; `mv dia?.log proyecto/src/`; `rm -r basura`.
lpie-ficheros.solution_summary: `mkdir -p` creates the whole path, `cp -r` copies folders with their contents, `mv` renames or moves, and `rm -r` deletes recursively. The `?` wildcard matches exactly one character, so `dia?.log` does not catch `dia10.log` or `dia11.log`.

lpie-comprimir.title: Archiving and compressing with tar, bzip2, and zip
lpie-comprimir.briefing:
You are asked to prepare several packages from what is in the directory:
1. Create `copia.tar.gz`: a gzip-compressed tar containing the entire `docs/` folder.
2. Compress `grande.txt` with bzip2. It should become `grande.txt.bz2` and the original should disappear.
3. From the `paquete.tar` archive extract only `config/red.conf`, nothing else.
4. Create `para-windows.zip` containing the `docs/` folder and everything inside it.
Your terminal opens in the challenge directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r010-comprimir`); files requested without a path go there.
lpie-comprimir.blind_alert: REQUEST [ARCHIVES] · You need to prepare compressed copies in three different formats and recover a single file from a package.
hints: Three tools, three formats: tar with gzip compression, bzip2 on a single file, and zip for exchanging with other systems. Extracting a single file from a tar is a matter of telling it which one.

`tar` combines creating, compressing, and naming the archive in one option; to extract, specify the member name exactly as it appears in the tar (see it with the listing option). `zip` needs an option to walk folders.
`tar czf copia.tar.gz docs`; `bzip2 grande.txt`; `tar xf paquete.tar config/red.conf`; `zip -r para-windows.zip docs`.
lpie-comprimir.solution_summary: `tar czf` creates a gzip-compressed tar, `bzip2` replaces the file with its `.bz2` version, `tar xf archive member` extracts only that member, and `zip -r` packages folders recursively.

lpie-redirecciones.title: Redirecting output and errors, and pipes
lpie-redirecciones.briefing:
You are asked to handle text streams:
1. Run `ls /etc/hostname /no/existe` in a single command and save the normal output to `bien.txt` and the error message to `mal.txt`.
2. Append the line `FIN` to the end of `bien.txt` without erasing what it already has.
3. Save to `top3.txt` the first three lines of `nombres.txt` after sorting alphabetically, using a pipe.
4. Save to `palabras.txt` only the number of words in `nombres.txt`.
Your terminal opens in the challenge directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r010-redirecciones`); files requested without a path go there.
lpie-redirecciones.blind_alert: REQUEST [PROCESSING] · You need to separate a command's normal output from its errors and extract data from a list using pipes.
hints: Standard output and error output are two different streams and each has its own redirection operator. To append without overwriting there is another operator.
The error stream is file descriptor 2. For item 3, the output of a sorting command goes to another command that cuts lines from the beginning. If `wc` reads from stdin, it does not print a filename.
`ls /etc/hostname /no/existe > bien.txt 2> mal.txt`; `echo FIN >> bien.txt`; `sort nombres.txt | head -n 3 > top3.txt`; `wc -w < nombres.txt > palabras.txt`.
lpie-redirecciones.solution_summary: `>` redirects standard output and `2>` redirects error output; `>>` appends to the end. With `sort … | head -n 3`, the first command's output feeds the second. `wc -w < file` reads from stdin, so it prints only the number.

checks.top3.txt: los tres primeros en el orden: top3.txt has the first three in the requested order

lpie-grep.title: Filtering an inventory with grep and regular expressions
lpie-grep.briefing:
The file `inventario.txt` has one line per item (and some comment lines). You are asked to extract:
1. Into `cables.txt`, the lines that contain the word `cable`, ignoring case.
2. Into `sin-stock.txt`, the lines of items with stock exactly 0 (stock is the last number; 10 or 30 do not count).
3. Into `no-comentarios.txt`, all lines that do not start with `#`.
4. Into `n-teclados.txt`, only the number of lines that contain `teclado`.
Your terminal opens in the challenge directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r010-grep`); files requested without a path go there.
lpie-grep.blind_alert: REQUEST [SEARCH] · You need to extract subsets of an inventory file according to text patterns.
hints: Everything is solved with the pattern search tool: one option ignores case, another inverts the selection, and another counts instead of showing. The start- and end-of-line anchors have their own symbols.

For "stock 0" you need the end-of-line anchor and something that prevents matching `10` or `30` (the 0 is preceded by a space). For "does not start with", invert the search for lines that start with `#`.
`grep -i cable inventario.txt > cables.txt`; `grep ' 0$' inventario.txt > sin-stock.txt`; `grep -v '^#' inventario.txt > no-comentarios.txt`; `grep -c teclado inventario.txt > n-teclados.txt`.
lpie-grep.solution_summary: `grep -i` ignores case, `' 0$'` anchors the 0 to the end of the line preceded by a space (so it does not catch `10` or `30`), `-v '^#'` inverts the search for lines starting with `#`, and `-c` returns the count.

checks.sin-stock.txt: las 2 líneas acabadas en: sin-stock.txt has the 2 lines ending in 0 (not the stock 10 line)

lpie-script.title: Writing a script that greets each argument
lpie-script.briefing:
Write a script `saluda.sh`, make it executable, and ensure it meets the following:
- Its first line is the interpreter `#!/bin/bash`.
- If run without arguments, it prints `uso: saluda.sh NOMBRE...` and exits with status 1.
- If it receives arguments, it prints `Hola NOMBRE` for each one, on separate lines, using a `for` loop, and exits with status 0.
For example, `./saluda.sh Ana Luis` must print `Hola Ana` and `Hola Luis`.
Your terminal opens in the challenge directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r010-script`); files requested without a path go there.
lpie-script.blind_alert: REQUEST [AUTOMATION] · A small shell utility that greets the people given to it is missing.
hints: Three pieces: the interpreter shebang, a condition on the number of arguments, and a loop that goes through all arguments. Don't forget the execute permission.
The number of arguments and the list of all of them are in special shell variables (`$#` and `$@`). The exit status is set with `exit`. Quote the list to respect arguments with spaces.
`#!/bin/bash`, then `if [ $# -eq 0 ]; then echo "uso: saluda.sh NOMBRE..."; exit 1; fi`, then `for n in "$@"; do echo "Hola $n"; done; exit 0`, and finally `chmod +x saluda.sh`.
lpie-script.solution_summary: The script checks `$#`; if it is 0, it prints the usage and exits with `exit 1`. Otherwise, `for n in "$@"` iterates over each argument and prints `Hola $n`, and ends with `exit 0`. `chmod +x` makes it executable and the `#!/bin/bash` line sets the interpreter.

checks../saluda.sh Ana Luis escribe Hola Ana y: ./saluda.sh Ana Luis prints Hola Ana and Hola Luis
checks.con argumentos sale con código 0: with arguments it exits with status 0
checks.sin argumentos sale con código 1 y expli: without arguments it exits with status 1 and explains usage

lpie-usuarios.title: Creating and removing accounts and groups
lpie-usuarios.briefing:
You are asked to manage accounts (you need `sudo`):
1. Create the group `ventas`.
2. Create the user `pedro` with home directory `/home/pedro`, shell `/bin/bash`, and `ventas` as a secondary group.
3. Save to `pedro.txt` only the line for `pedro` in `/etc/passwd`.
4. Save to `id.txt` the output of `id pedro`.
5. Remove the account `antiguo` (it already exists) along with its home directory.
Your terminal opens in the challenge directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r010-usuarios`); files requested without a path go there.
lpie-usuarios.blind_alert: REQUEST [ACCOUNTS] · You need to add a new person to a group and remove an account that is no longer used.
hints: Creating and removing groups and users with the account administration commands, and two files that document the result. Everything requires privileges except writing in your directory.

`useradd` has options to create the home directory, set the shell, and add secondary groups. Removal with deletion of the home directory is an option of `userdel`. To extract a line from `/etc/passwd`, filter by the beginning of the line.
`sudo groupadd ventas`; `sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash -G ventas pedro`; `grep '^pedro:' /etc/passwd > pedro.txt`; `id pedro > id.txt`; `sudo userdel -r antiguo`.
lpie-usuarios.solution_summary: `groupadd` creates the group; `useradd -m -s /bin/bash -G ventas pedro` creates the account, home, shell, and secondary group; `userdel -r` deletes the user and home directory. The line from `/etc/passwd` is extracted with `grep '^pedro:'`, and `id` shows uid, gid, and groups.

lpie-permisos.title: Permissions and ownership in numeric and symbolic modes
lpie-permisos.briefing:
The user `luis` and the group `contabilidad` already exist (you need `sudo` to change owners). You are asked to adjust:
1. `informe.txt` must end up with permissions 640 (use numeric mode).
2. `copia.sh` must be executable only by its owner, without touching the rest of the permissions (symbolic mode).
3. `informe.txt` must belong to user `luis` and group `contabilidad`, with a single command.
4. The folder `privado/` must end up with 700.
5. Remove the read permission for "others" from `notas.txt`.
Your terminal opens in the challenge directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r010-permisos`); files requested without a path go there.
lpie-permisos.blind_alert: REQUEST [PERMISSIONS] · Several department files have permissions and owners that do not match.
hints: Two ways to express permissions, numeric and symbolic, and a separate command for owner and group. Check the initial state with `ls -l` before changing anything.
In symbolic mode you indicate who (`u`, `g`, `o`), whether to add or remove (`+`/`-`), and which permission. The ownership command accepts user and group together separated by a colon.
`chmod 640 informe.txt`; `chmod u+x copia.sh`; `sudo chown luis:contabilidad informe.txt`; `chmod 700 privado`; `chmod o-r notas.txt`.
lpie-permisos.solution_summary: `chmod 640` and `chmod 700` set permissions in octal; `chmod u+x` adds execute only for the owner and `chmod o-r` removes read from others. `chown luis:contabilidad` changes user and group at once (requires root).

checks.copia.sh tiene 744 (solo el propietario: copia.sh has mode 744 (only the owner can execute)

lpie-especiales.title: Group directory with SGID, sticky bit, and a symbolic link
lpie-especiales.briefing:
The `equipo` group needs a shared directory, `compartido/` (you need `sudo` to change the group):
1. Make `equipo` the group owner of `compartido/`.
2. Give rwx to the owner and the group and no permissions to others.
3. Enable the SGID bit so files created inside inherit the `equipo` group.
4. Enable the sticky bit so each user can only delete their own files, as in `/tmp`.
5. Create a symbolic link named `atajo` that points to `compartido`.
Your terminal opens in the task directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r010-especiales`); files requested without a path go there.
lpie-especiales.blind_alert: REQUEST [COLLABORATION] · A team needs a shared directory where each member can only delete their own files.
hints: Combine a group change, base permissions, two special permissions, and a symbolic link. Special permissions can be added with symbolic mode or with a leading fourth octal digit.

The group is changed with `chgrp` or `chown`. SGID is `g+s` and sticky is `o+t`; in octal the extra digit is 2 and 1 respectively. In a symbolic link, the first argument is the target and the second is the link name.
`sudo chgrp equipo compartido`; `chmod 770 compartido`; `chmod g+s compartido`; `chmod o+t compartido` (or `chmod 3770 compartido`); `ln -s compartido atajo`.
lpie-especiales.solution_summary: `chgrp` sets the group; `chmod 770` gives rwx to owner and group; `g+s` (SGID) makes new items inherit the group and `o+t` (sticky) restricts deletion to the owner. `ln -s compartido atajo` creates the symbolic link (target first).

checks.compartido/ es del grupo equipo: compartido/ is owned by the equipo group
checks.compartido/ tiene rwxrwx--- (sin contar: compartido/ has rwxrwx--- (not counting the special bits)
checks.atajo es un enlace simbólico a compartid: atajo is a symbolic link to compartido

lpie-comillas-variables.title: Local and exported variables and quoting: what a child process inherits
lpie-comillas-variables.briefing:
You are asked to demonstrate how variables and quoting behave:
1. Create the local variable `saludo` with the value `hola` without exporting it, and the variable `ORDEN` with the value `desc` exported.
2. Launch a child `bash` that prints on a single line the value of `saludo` and the value of `ORDEN`, each in brackets, and save the output to `hijo.txt`. It should be `[][desc]`.
3. Save to `entorno.txt` only the line that `env` shows for `ORDEN`. Then remove `ORDEN` from the shell and save to `borrada.txt` the output of `echo "[$ORDEN]"` (it should be `[]`).
4. Save to `ls.txt` the path to the `ls` program and to `cd.txt` what the shell says about `cd`.
5. Create `comillas.txt` with two lines that contain the literal text `$HOME` unexpanded: the first using single quotes and the second using double quotes with the `$` escaped.
Your terminal opens in the task directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r010-comillas-variables`); files requested without a path go there.
lpie-comillas-variables.blind_alert: REQUEST [ENVIRONMENT] · Demonstrate which shell variables reach a child process and how quoting affects them.
hints: A variable only reaches the child if it is exported; single quotes prevent expansion and double quotes allow it unless you escape the `$`. Every part demonstrates that difference.

To have the child expand the `$` and not your shell, pass the command to the child in single quotes. Remember that in `saludo=hola` there are no spaces around the `=`. `which` gives a program's path and `type` explains what a command is.

`saludo=hola; export ORDEN=desc`; `bash -c 'echo "[$saludo][$ORDEN]"' > hijo.txt`; `env | grep '^ORDEN=' > entorno.txt`; `unset ORDEN; echo "[${ORDEN-}]" > borrada.txt`; `which ls > ls.txt; type cd > cd.txt`; `printf '%s\n' '$HOME' "\$HOME" > comillas.txt`.
lpie-comillas-variables.solution_summary: `export` copies the variable to the children's environment; `saludo` without exporting does not arrive and the child prints `[]`. `unset` removes the variable. Single quotes leave `$HOME` literal, and in double quotes you have to escape the `$` (`\$HOME`) to achieve the same.

checks.entorno.txt: solo la línea ORDEN=desc de: entorno.txt: only the ORDEN=desc line from env

lpie-almacenamiento-datos.title: Where data is stored: executables, /etc, /proc, and the disk
lpie-almacenamiento-datos.briefing:
You are asked to collect information from several system sources:
1. Save to `rutas.txt` the path to the `ps` executable and the path to `cut`, one per line.
2. Save to `etc.txt` only the line for the `root` user in `/etc/passwd`.
3. Save to `memoria.txt` only the `MemTotal` line from `/proc/meminfo`.
4. Save to `montaje.txt` the mount point where `/tmp` is located (last column of the data line from `df -P /tmp`).
5. Save to `tamano.txt` only the number of MiB that the `datos/` directory occupies according to `du -sm`.
Your terminal opens in the task directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r010-almacenamiento-datos`); files requested without a path go there.
lpie-almacenamiento-datos.blind_alert: REQUEST [INVENTORY] · You need to document where programs, configuration, kernel data, and disk space reside.
hints: Each part reads from a different place: the PATH, a configuration file, the kernel's virtual filesystem, and disk space utilities. Extract only what is requested.

`which` locates executables. `grep` with a start-of-line anchor extracts an entry from `/etc/passwd` or `/proc/meminfo`. In `df -P` output, the data line is the second one and the mount point is the sixth column. `du -sm` prints size and name: keep the first field.

`{ which ps; which cut; } > rutas.txt`; `grep '^root:' /etc/passwd > etc.txt`; `grep '^MemTotal:' /proc/meminfo > memoria.txt`; `df -P /tmp | awk 'NR==2{print $6}' > montaje.txt`; `du -sm datos | cut -f1 > tamano.txt`.
lpie-almacenamiento-datos.solution_summary: Executables are located with `which`; `/etc/passwd` stores accounts; `/proc/meminfo` is live kernel information; `df -P` gives the mount point in column 6 and `du -sm | cut -f1` the size in MiB.

lpie-almacenamiento-datos2.title: Processes: PID, /proc/PID, and ps
lpie-almacenamiento-datos2.briefing:
You are asked to create a process and inspect it in different ways:
1. Launch `sleep 1234` in the background with `&` and save its PID to `pid.txt`.
2. Read the program name of that PID from `/proc/PID/comm` and save only the name to `comm.txt`.
3. Save to `ps.txt` the PID and the name that `ps` shows for that process, without headers.
4. Save to `estado.txt` only the first letter of the process state according to `ps` (the STAT column).

lpie-almacenamiento-datos2.blind_alert: REQUEST [PROCESSES] · You need to launch a background process and document its identity from several sources.
hints: The process must remain alive while you request its data. A special shell variable gives you its PID as soon as you launch it, and from there you inspect it through `/proc` and `ps`.

Save the PID with `echo $! > pid.txt` right after launching it. The name is in a file inside the `/proc/<PID>/` directory. With the `ps` output option that ends in `=` headers are omitted; for the first letter use `cut -c1`.
`sleep 1234 &` and `echo $! > pid.txt`; `cat /proc/$(cat pid.txt)/comm > comm.txt`; `ps -p $(cat pid.txt) -o pid=,comm= > ps.txt`; `ps -o stat= -p $(cat pid.txt) | tr -d ' ' | cut -c1 > estado.txt`.
lpie-almacenamiento-datos2.solution_summary: `sleep 1234 &` creates the process and `$!` gives its PID. `/proc/PID/comm` contains the program name, `ps -p PID -o pid=,comm=` prints PID and name without a header, and `ps -o stat=` shows the state (S = sleeping), from which the first letter is taken.

lpie-red-basica.title: Basic host networking: loopback, localhost, DNS, and resolution order
lpie-red-basica.briefing:
You are asked to document the basic network configuration of the host:
1. Save to `lo.txt` the brief output of the addresses of the loopback interface `lo`.
2. Save to `resuelve.txt` only the IPv4 address with which the system resolves `localhost`.
3. Save to `hosts.txt` the first line of `/etc/hosts` that mentions `localhost`.
4. Save to `dns.txt` only the IP of the first `nameserver` in `/etc/resolv.conf`.
5. Save to `orden.txt` the `hosts:` line from `/etc/nsswitch.conf`, which indicates the order in which names are resolved.
Your terminal opens in the task directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r010-red-basica`); files requested without a path go there.
lpie-red-basica.blind_alert: REQUEST [NETWORK] · You need to document the basic network configuration of a host: local interface, names, and DNS servers.
hints: Five network checks: one on the interface tools, one on the system's name resolution, and three on configuration files. Extract only the requested line or field.

`ip` has a brief output option and can be limited to one interface. `getent` queries resolution the way the system would (there is an IPv4 variant). For DNS, filter the lines that start with `nameserver` and take the second field of the first one.

`ip -br addr show lo > lo.txt`; `getent ahostsv4 localhost | awk 'NR==1{print $1}' > resuelve.txt`; `grep -m1 localhost /etc/hosts > hosts.txt`; `awk '/^nameserver/{print $2; exit}' /etc/resolv.conf > dns.txt`; `grep '^hosts:' /etc/nsswitch.conf > orden.txt`.
lpie-red-basica.solution_summary: `ip -br addr show lo` shows the loopback interface in brief format, `getent ahostsv4` resolves as the system does, `/etc/hosts` maps local names, `/etc/resolv.conf` lists the DNS servers, and the `hosts:` line in `nsswitch.conf` sets the order of the resolution sources.
